summary.title: Anti-If: The missing patterns
summary.one_liner: Five refactoring patterns (boolean params, polymorphism, null objects/Optional, inlining conditionals into expressions, and coping strategies like Ruby's Hash#fetch) that replace duplicated if statements with cleaner code.
takeaways: Boolean parameters usually signal two methods bundled into one; split them into two named methods.
Switch statements on type are risky when repeated; polymorphism ensures new types get their behaviour.
Use Null Object, Optional, or an empty collection instead of passing null around.
Tolerance matters: a single unduplicated if is usually fine, and validation belongs at the edges of the system.
Push repeated 'no result' checks into one place by giving callers a coping strategy, such as Hash#fetch's default.
summary.summary: The article, by Joe Wright, argues that if statements, especially duplicated or nested ones, make code hard to read and change, because they hide domain concepts and force readers to simulate execution. It offers five patterns: Boolean Params, Switch to Polymorphism, NullObject/Optional over null passing, inlining statements into expressions, and giving a coping strategy. Each pattern has a context, problem, a tolerance level for when to use it, and a solution. The post stresses moderation: a single unduplicated if is usually fine, and validation belongs at system boundaries.
